introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s argument is simple and repeated: a field left to itself grows thorns, a flower needs a gardener, a child needs a teacher, and so humanity needs an educator, who must be more than human to educate it wholly. The readings name the Prophets as those gardeners. Much old wisdom stands with him: Proverbs passes the sluggard’s field, Confucius says practice sets people apart, Plato speaks of turning the soul to the light, Paul of milk before meat, the Mishnah of making oneself a teacher. But the claim that nature is defective and independence impossible has been disputed for as long, and the disputants are given their say: Mencius, for whom human nature runs to good like water downhill; Wordsworth’s child trailing clouds of glory; Emerson and Kant on trusting one’s own mind; the Buddha’s “be ye lamps unto yourselves”; and Darwin, who found grandeur in nature untended.
questions: “Independence is not possible,” yet “man has his own feelings and perceptions and can make new discoveries.” Where do Emerson’s “trust thyself” and the Buddha’s “be ye lamps unto yourselves” fit between those two sentences?

The readings say an uncultivated child would be like a wild animal; Wordsworth and Mencius see goodness that upbringing can spoil. What in your experience supports each, and what kind of education would satisfy both?
Socrates calls himself a midwife and Plato speaks of turning the soul toward the light. Is the Educator of these readings a giver of what was absent or an awakener of what was present?

“He must first ascertain their truth and then follow their directions.” How does a learner test a teacher, a physician or a captain before trusting them, and what would the equivalent be for a Prophet?
Kant thought enlightenment meant growing out of tutelage; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says even the elite need a commander. Is there a way of being taught that leaves a person more able to think, not less?

outside.why: “Man stands in need of an educator.” Paul’s figure for humanity before Christ is a child and heir who is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father.
The educator must be “distinguished above all men,” or he could not teach them. Matthew records what the crowds noticed first: he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.

The educator must be perfect in every way. Plato reached a similar demand by reason alone and doubted it could be met: until philosophers are kings, cities will never have rest from their evils. What does the reading supply that Plato could only wish for?
The flower has its innate capacity and still needs a gardener. Paul keeps both, and adds a third: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
“Acquired perfections … depend upon training.” Pope’s couplet is the proverb for it: just as the twig is bent, the tree’s inclined.
A lamp needs a kindler and “a mover and educator is necessary.” Socrates describes his own part in another’s understanding as a midwife’s: he brings to birth what he did not put there.
Hidden lights “come forth from the invisible realm.” Plato denies that education puts sight into blind eyes; the power is already in the soul and has to be turned toward the light.

Without the Educator the lights stay “like unto seeds concealed beneath the earth.” Browning’s Paracelsus says that to know is to open a way for an imprisoned splendour to escape, and not to let in a light from without. Is the teacher the source of the light or the one who frees it?
“He cannot dispense with teacher and educator.” The traveller reading Isaiah in his chariot says the same of himself: how can I, except some man should guide me?
“Independence is not possible.” Emerson’s essay on self-reliance says the opposite in three words: trust thyself. What does each fear will be lost if the other is believed?

The soldier follows the general and the passenger the captain. Tennyson’s Light Brigade also followed: theirs not to reason why, when someone had blundered. The reading adds that one “must first ascertain their truth.” How is that done?

Under real teachers “all will be manifested and made known.” The Qur’án describes the Messenger’s work in these terms: he teacheth you the Scripture and wisdom, and teacheth you that which ye knew not.
A teacher is needed “to open his eyes and ears as they should be opened.” Isaiah’s promise: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
Every creature needs instruction, so the creature “is not perfect.” Confucius on what instruction does to an equal start: by nature men are nearly alike; by practice they get to be wide apart.

“The world of nature is incomplete, imperfect until awakened … by education.” Darwin closes the Origin of Species finding grandeur in nature left to itself, from which endless forms most beautiful have been evolved. Do the two disagree about nature, or about what counts as perfection?

A plot left to itself “would become a field of thorns and useless weeds.” Proverbs went by such a field: it was all grown over with thorns, and the stone wall was broken down; then I saw, and received instruction.

Schools exist to “rescue and redeem” man from the defects of nature. Gray, watching schoolboys at play, doubts the gift: where ignorance is bliss, ’tis folly to be wise. What does education cost the one who receives it?
The human world needs guidance more than the lower creatures do. The psalm offers instruction and asks not to be resisted: be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding.

Man is set above the three lower kingdoms. Mencius held that the difference is but small, and that the mass of people cast it away while superior men preserve it. Is education mainly adding something, or keeping what is easily lost?
Every kingdom “must be cultivated in order to reach its fulfillment.” The vinedresser of John’s Gospel prunes even the branch that bears, that it may bring forth more fruit.

Children without cultivation “would become like wild animals.” Wordsworth’s child arrives trailing clouds of glory, and it is growing up that closes the shades of the prison-house upon him. Which account matches the children you have known?
The need for schooling proves “that the world of nature must be developed.” Aquinas’s maxim keeps nature and its completion together: grace does not destroy nature but perfects it.

The readings find defect in nature. Mencius argued that human nature tends to good as water flows downward, and that people are made to do evil only as water is forced uphill. Does education correct a defect or clear an obstruction?
Whoever educates children by the Prophets’ teachings “has followed the Prophets.” Jesus: suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me.
“This world is like unto an orchard, there must needs be a gardener.” Candide ends with people who have given up on finding one: we must take care of our garden. How far can that modest programme go?

One education prevents open crime, the other “both obvious and hidden.” Confucius: led by laws and punishments, the people avoid them and have no shame; led by virtue, they have a sense of shame and become good.
“The gaining of Wisdom requires a teacher.” The Mishnah makes it a first rule of life: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a companion.
A place of refuse was planted during days of danger and is now a garden. Isaiah: instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier the myrtle.
“The gardeners of the world of humanity are the Prophets of God.” Paul to the Corinthians: we are labourers together with God; ye are God’s husbandry.

The divine Gardeners “till the earth of human hearts.” The Dhammapada gives the tools to the person: well-makers lead the water, fletchers bend the arrow, carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.
“Without an educator, a human being does not become truly human.” Aristotle: man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but, when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all.

The readings exalt the educator. Mencius warns about the wish to be one: the evil of men is that they like to be teachers of others. How is a true educator told from someone who merely likes the role?

Asked whether progress will not make prophets unnecessary, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers that mankind needs “a universal motive power.” Kant defined enlightenment as leaving a self-incurred tutelage: dare to use your own understanding. Is needing an educator a stage, or a permanent condition?

Those who say “We are among the elite and need no education” are like officers who want no commander. The Buddha’s last counsel to his monks: be ye lamps unto yourselves; look not for refuge to any one besides yourselves. Was he speaking to the kind of people the reading rebukes?

The Báb’s sentence follows the Qur’án closely: He hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own, to recite His revelations, to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom.
“People are observed to be as infants.” Paul to his converts: I have fed you with milk, and not with meat, for hitherto ye were not able to bear it.
Black soil is covered with flowers by sun, rain and wind. Isaiah makes the rain a figure for teaching: it watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud; so shall my word be.
The sun speaks to the earth: “I am training thee.” Francis of Assisi praises God through Brother Sun, who brings the day, and through Mother Earth, who sustains and brings forth fruits and flowers.
“Bestow upon it a new existence.” The voice from the throne at the end of the Bible: behold, I make all things new.
Nature “is imperfect and needs education.” Milton’s definition of the end of learning starts from the same lack: to repair the ruins of our first parents by regaining to know God aright.
Man “has not created himself”; the deficiencies of the contingent world point to a perfect source. Aquinas’s second way argues likewise from causes that cannot cause themselves to a first cause.
